stem: Scientists examined water samples from different water springs. For these samples, the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in a closed system (limited carbon dioxide supply) had a minimum of 0.014 atmosphere (atm) and a maximum of 0.180 atm. The partial pressure of carbon dioxide in an open system (unlimited carbon dioxide supply) had a minimum of 0.00049 atm and a maximum of 0.05900 atm. Which statement best compares the range of the partial pressure of carbon dioxide for closed systems and open systems?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The range for closed systems is less than the range for open systems.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The range for closed systems is greater than the range for open systems.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The ranges are equal.

choices.label: D
choices.content: There is not enough information to compare the ranges.

whyCorrect: The range of a data set is maximum minus minimum, and both a maximum and a minimum are given for each system, so you have everything you need. Closed: 0.180 − 0.014 = 0.166 atm. Open: 0.05900 − 0.00049 = 0.05851 atm. 0.166 is bigger than 0.0585, so the closed-system range is greater.

whyWrong.A: This reverses the comparison. The open-system numbers have more decimal places, which makes them look more precise, but 0.05851 is still much smaller than 0.166.
whyWrong.C: The two differences are not equal — 0.166 against 0.05851, almost three times apart.
whyWrong.D: A range needs only the maximum and the minimum, and both are stated for both systems. You never need the individual data values.

stem: Ari examined a set of 86 plants. The lightest plant has a mass of 2.8 kilograms (kg) and the heaviest plant has a mass of 6.2 kg. Chihiro examined the same set of 86 plants and also an additional plant with a mass of 11.7 kg. Which of the following must be true about the set of plants that Ari examined and the set of plants that Chihiro examined?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The standard deviation of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Ari examined is greater than the standard deviation of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Chihiro examined.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The range of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Ari examined is greater than the range of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Chihiro examined.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The median of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Ari examined is less than the median of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Chihiro examined.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The mean of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Ari examined is less than the mean of the masses, in kg, of the plants that Chihiro examined.

whyCorrect: Every one of Ari's 86 masses is at most 6.2 kg, so Ari's mean is at most 6.2. Chihiro's set is Ari's set plus a single 11.7 kg plant, and adding a value that sits above the current mean always pulls the mean up. That argument works no matter what the 86 individual masses are, which is what "must be true" demands.

whyWrong.A: Backwards. The extra 11.7 kg plant sits far outside the 2.8–6.2 kg spread of the rest, so it increases the spread; Chihiro's standard deviation is the larger one.
whyWrong.B: Also backwards. Ari's range is 6.2 − 2.8 = 3.4 kg; Chihiro's is 11.7 − 2.8 = 8.9 kg.
whyWrong.C: The median can only move up or stay put, and "must be true" rules this out because it can stay put. Ari's median is the average of the 43rd and 44th masses; Chihiro's is the 44th. If those two masses are equal — entirely possible — the two medians are the same, so "less than" is not guaranteed.

stem: An environmental scientist is investigating the volatility of 175 organic compounds by finding the boiling point of each compound. The mean boiling point of all 175 compounds is 167 degrees Celsius. The scientist classifies each of these compounds as either semivolatile or volatile. Of the 175 compounds, 50 compounds were classified as semivolatile, and these 50 compounds have a mean boiling point of 327 degrees Celsius. The remaining 125 compounds were classified as volatile. What is the mean boiling point, in degrees Celsius, of the 125 compounds classified as volatile compounds?
whyCorrect: Means do not combine by averaging — work with totals. The 175 compounds have a combined boiling point total of 175 × 167 = 29,225. The 50 semivolatile ones account for 50 × 327 = 16,350. So the 125 volatile compounds total 29,225 − 16,350 = 12,875, and their mean is 12,875 ÷ 125 = 103 degrees Celsius.

Data set \(F\) consists of 55 integers, where the value of each integer is between 150 and 260. Data set \(G\) consists of the same 55 integers in \(F\) as well as the integer 10. Which of the following must be less for data set \(G\) than for data set \(F\)?

I. The mean
II. The median

choices.label: B
choices.content: II only

choices.label: C
choices.content: I and II

choices.label: D
choices.content: Neither I nor II

whyCorrect: The mean must fall, because 10 is below every value in \(F\) and so certainly below \(F\)'s mean; adding a value below the mean always pulls it down. The median need not fall. \(F\) has 55 values, so its median is the 28th; \(G\) has 56, so its median is the average of \(G\)'s 28th and 29th, which are \(F\)'s 27th and 28th. If \(F\)'s 27th and 28th values happen to be equal — nothing forbids it, since the integers may repeat — that average equals \(F\)'s median, so it is not less. "Must be less" fails for II.

whyWrong.C: I is right but II is not guaranteed — repeated values around the middle position let the median stay exactly where it was.
whyWrong.D: The mean genuinely must decrease: 10 is far below every one of the 55 values, so it cannot leave the average unchanged or raise it.

stem: A survey of the daily commuting times, in minutes, of seven different Chicago-based employees at a certain company yielded a data set consisting of the values 31, 13, 44, 32, 53, 22, and 44. A survey of the daily commuting times, in minutes, of seven different San Francisco-based employees at the same company yielded a data set consisting of the values 46, 31, 19, 33, 48, \(x\), and 38. If the means of the two data sets are equal, what is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Both data sets have 7 values, so equal means is the same as equal totals — you never have to divide. The Chicago total is 31 + 13 + 44 + 32 + 53 + 22 + 44 = 239. The six known San Francisco values total 46 + 31 + 19 + 33 + 48 + 38 = 215. So \(x = 239 - 215 = 24\).

A company conducted a study concerning the time spent on extracurricular activities by students in grades 6, 7, and 8 and their level of school spirit. A total of 90 students were selected at random from all students in grades 6, 7, and 8 in a large school district in the US. The selected students were asked to report their level of school spirit as either low, medium, or high. The table summarizes the distribution of the selected students by grade.
Grade678
Number of students302634
If the results of the study suggest a relationship between the self-reported level of school spirit and the amount of time spent on extracurricular activities by students in grades 6, 7, and 8, which of the following aspects of the study will prevent the results from being generalized to all students in grades 6, 7, and 8 in the US?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The selected students are not all from the same school.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The number of selected students is too small.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The number of selected students from each grade is different.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The students were not selected at random from all students in grades 6, 7, and 8.

whyCorrect: A result generalizes only to the population the sample was randomly drawn from. Here the random draw was made inside one large school district, so the population it represents is that district — not every 6th, 7th and 8th grader in the US. Students outside the district had no chance of being selected, and no sample size fixes that.

whyWrong.A: Drawing from several schools makes a sample broader, not narrower. It is a strength, not the flaw.
whyWrong.B: 90 is a workable sample size, and in any case sample size affects the margin of error, not which population the result applies to.
whyWrong.C: The grade counts are close to even, and unequal group sizes within a random sample are normal; they do not block generalization.

stem: A machine fills bags with approximately 10 ounces of cranberries. To test the accuracy of the filling process, 148 bags of cranberries were selected at random and weighed. Based on the sample, it is estimated that the average weight of all bags of cranberries filled by the machine in an 8-hour period is 9.89 ounces, with an associated margin of error of 0.14 ounce. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this estimate?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Plausible values for the average weight of all bags of cranberries filled by the machine are between 9.75 ounces and 10.03 ounces.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Plausible values for the average weight of all bags of cranberries filled by the machine are less than 9.75 ounces or greater than 10.03 ounces.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The average weight of all bags of cranberries filled by the machine is greater than 9.99 ounces.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The average weight of all bags of cranberries filled by the machine is less than 9.99 ounces.

whyCorrect: A margin of error marks off an interval on either side of the estimate, and the values inside that interval are the plausible ones. Here that is 9.89 − 0.14 = 9.75 up to 9.89 + 0.14 = 10.03 ounces.

whyWrong.B: This has the interval inside out. Values further than 0.14 from the estimate are the implausible ones.
whyWrong.C: 9.99 is 9.89 + 0.10, which is not either endpoint, and a margin of error never lets you claim the true average lies on one side of a single number.
whyWrong.D: Same problem: the estimate supports a two-sided interval, not a one-sided claim, and 9.99 is not an endpoint of it.

stem: A town manager selected 2 random samples of residents in the town to estimate the percentage of all residents that planned to vote in favor of a new business in the downtown area. Based on the first sample, he estimated that 75% of the residents in town planned to vote in favor, with an associated margin of error of 8.3%. Based on the second sample, he estimated that 83% of the residents in the town planned to vote in favor, with an associated margin of error of 6.7%. Assuming the margins of error were calculated the same way, which of the following best explains why the first sample obtained a larger margin of error than the second sample?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The first sample contained fewer residents than the second sample.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The first sample contained more residents than the second sample.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The first sample contained a lower percentage of residents that planned to vote in favor of a new business in the downtown area.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The first sample contained a higher percentage of residents that planned to vote in favor of a new business in the downtown area.

whyCorrect: Margin of error shrinks as the sample gets bigger — more people surveyed means a more precise estimate. The first sample's margin of error is the larger one (8.3% against 6.7%), so the first sample must have been the smaller one.

whyWrong.B: This has the relationship backwards. A larger sample produces a smaller margin of error, not a larger one.
whyWrong.C: The estimated percentage itself is not what drives the size of the margin of error here; the question says the margins were calculated the same way, leaving sample size as the explanation.
whyWrong.D: Same issue, and it is also false as stated — the first sample's percentage was 75%, lower than the second sample's 83%.

stem: A district board in a certain state is proposing a change to the time school starts to all high schools in the district. A sample of 353 high school students were selected from all high school students in the district. The selected students were asked if they approved of the proposed change, and 300 students responded that they did not approve. Which of the following is the largest population that the results of the survey can be generalized?

choices.label: A
choices.content: All high school students in the district

choices.label: B
choices.content: The 353 students who were surveyed

choices.label: C
choices.content: The 300 students that responded that they did not approve of the proposed change

choices.label: D
choices.content: All high school students in the state

whyCorrect: The results generalize to the group the sample was drawn from, and no further. The 353 students were selected from all high school students in the district, so that district-wide group is the largest population the survey speaks for.

whyWrong.B: The whole point of sampling is to say something about a group larger than the sample itself, so this is not the largest population.
whyWrong.C: This is a subset of the sample, smaller still, and it is defined by the answer given — not a population you would generalize to at all.
whyWrong.D: Students in other districts had no chance of being selected, so the survey says nothing about the state as a whole.

stem: A company that produces only one type of item wants to estimate the percent of the items produced in a typical week that are defective. A random sample of 400 of the items produced in a certain week were tested. Based on the sample, it is estimated that 8.5% of all items produced by the company in this week were defective, with an associated margin of error of 2.73%. Based on the estimate and associated margin of error, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all items produced by the company during this week?

choices.label: A
choices.content: 2.73% of all items are defective.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It is plausible that between 5.77% and 11.23% of the items are defective.

choices.label: C
choices.content: 8.5% of all items are defective.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It is plausible that more than 11.23% of the items are defective.

whyCorrect: The estimate plus and minus the margin of error gives the interval of plausible values: 8.5 − 2.73 = 5.77% and 8.5 + 2.73 = 11.23%. The conclusion has to be stated as a plausible range, because a sample can only narrow the possibilities, never pin down the true percent.

whyWrong.A: 2.73% is the margin of error, the width on either side of the estimate — not a defect rate.
whyWrong.C: 8.5% is the sample's estimate. Reporting it as the exact figure for all items throws away the margin of error, which exists precisely because the sample may miss.
whyWrong.D: 11.23% is the top of the plausible range, so values above it are the implausible ones.

stem: To estimate the proportion of a population that has a certain characteristic, a random sample was selected from the population. Based on the sample, it is estimated that the proportion of the population that has the characteristic is 0.2, with an associated margin of error of 0.08. Based on this estimate and margin of error, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about the proportion of the population that has the characteristic?

choices.label: A
choices.content: It is plausible that the proportion is between 0.12 and 0.28.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It is plausible that the proportion is less than 0.12.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The proportion is exactly 0.2.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It is plausible that the proportion is greater than 0.28.

whyCorrect: Subtract and add the margin of error to the estimate: 0.2 − 0.08 = 0.12 and 0.2 + 0.08 = 0.28. Everything inside that interval is plausible; everything outside it is not supported by the sample.

whyWrong.B: 0.12 is the bottom end of the plausible interval, so proportions below it are the ones the estimate argues against.
whyWrong.C: 0.2 is a sample estimate, not a measurement of the whole population. If it were exact there would be no reason to report a margin of error.
whyWrong.D: 0.28 is the top end of the interval, so values above it fall outside the plausible range.

stem: The manager of a gym selected a sample of 139 members at random to estimate the percentage of the gym's members that would continue to pay for a membership if the price increased. From the survey, the manager estimates that 82% of the gym's members would continue to pay for membership if the price increased, with an associated margin of error of 6.39%. If the survey is repeated with a random sample of 278 members and the results are calculated in the same way, which of the following will be the most likely effect of using the larger random sample compared to the smaller random sample?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The margin of error will be lower

choices.label: B
choices.content: The margin of error will be higher

choices.label: C
choices.content: The estimate of the percentage of the gym's members that would continue to pay for a membership if the price increased will be lower

choices.label: D
choices.content: The estimate of the percentage of the gym's members that would continue to pay for a membership if the price increased will be higher

whyCorrect: Surveying more people gives a more precise estimate, and precision is exactly what the margin of error measures. Doubling the sample from 139 to 278 therefore shrinks the margin of error. Note the direction: bigger sample, smaller margin.

whyWrong.B: This is the relationship inverted. Small samples are the unreliable ones, so they carry the larger margins of error.
whyWrong.C: A larger sample changes how precise the estimate is, not which way it points. There is no reason for the percentage itself to fall.
whyWrong.D: Same reason — the estimate could come out slightly higher or slightly lower, so neither direction is "most likely". Only the margin of error has a predictable direction.

stem: A machine fills bags with approximately 29 ounces of walnuts. To test the accuracy of the filling process, 169 bags of walnuts were selected at random and weighed. Based on the sample, it is estimated that the average weight of all bags of walnuts filled by the machine in an 8-hour period is 28.88 ounces, with an associated margin of error of 0.13 ounce. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this estimate?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Plausible values for the average weight of all bags of walnuts filled by the machine are between 28.75 ounces and 29.01 ounces.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Plausible values for the average weight of all bags of walnuts filled by the machine are less than 28.75 ounces or greater than 29.01 ounces.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The average weight of all bags of walnuts filled by the machine is less than 28.99 ounces.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The average weight of all bags of walnuts filled by the machine is greater than 28.99 ounces.

whyCorrect: Take the estimate and step the margin of error off in both directions: 28.88 − 0.13 = 28.75 and 28.88 + 0.13 = 29.01. Those two numbers bracket the plausible values for the true average.

whyWrong.B: This names the values outside the interval, which are the ones the estimate argues against.
whyWrong.C: 28.99 is not an endpoint of anything here, and a margin of error supports a two-sided interval rather than a one-sided claim.
whyWrong.D: Same problem in the other direction, and 28.99 does not come from 28.88 and 0.13 at all.

stem: A researcher is designing a study to investigate the average number of hours a student at a high school spends reading per day. The researcher will report the average number of hours a student at the high school spends reading with an associated margin of error. The researcher is considering using a random sample of either 105 or 210 students from the high school. Which of the following could be the most likely effect of using the larger random sample compared to the smaller random sample?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The reported margin of error would be lower.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The reported margin of error would be higher.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The reported average number of hours would be lower.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The reported average number of hours would be higher.

whyCorrect: A bigger sample estimates the population more precisely, and margin of error is the measure of that imprecision, so going from 105 students to 210 lowers it. Nothing about sample size predicts which way the average itself will come out.

whyWrong.B: Backwards — the smaller sample is the one with the larger margin of error.
whyWrong.C: The average could land above or below the smaller sample's figure. Sample size controls precision, not direction.
whyWrong.D: Same reason: no direction of change in the average is more likely than the other.

stem: A survey was conducted in Franklin to estimate the number of adult residents who supported the addition of a parking garage in their town. Based on the survey, it is estimated that 77% of all adult residents of Franklin support the addition of a parking garage in their town, with an associated margin of error of 5%. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all adult residents of Franklin?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Franklin who support the addition of a parking garage in their town are between 72% and 82%

choices.label: B
choices.content: The addition of a parking garage in the town is supported by exactly 72% of all adult residents of Franklin

choices.label: C
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Franklin who support the addition of a parking garage in their town are either less than 72% or more than 82%

choices.label: D
choices.content: The addition of a parking garage in the town is supported by more than 82% of all adult residents of Franklin

whyCorrect: Subtract and add the margin of error: 77 − 5 = 72 and 77 + 5 = 82. The survey supports the claim that the true percentage lies somewhere in that band, and says nothing more precise than that.

whyWrong.B: 72% is the low end of the interval, not a value the survey singles out, and a sample never establishes an exact population percentage.
whyWrong.C: This names everything outside the interval — the values the survey argues against, not for.
whyWrong.D: 82% is the top of the interval, so support above it is what the estimate rules out as unlikely.

stem: A research manager selected 2 random samples of ovens of a certain type to estimate the average amount of time this type of oven takes to preheat to 325 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The research manager recorded the amount of time, in minutes, each oven takes to preheat to 325°F. Based on the first sample, the research manager estimated that this type of oven takes an average of 15.2 minutes to preheat to 325°F, with an associated margin of error of 1 minute. Based on the second sample, the research manager estimated that this type of oven takes an average of 15.4 minutes to preheat to 325°F, with an associated margin of error of 2.2 minutes. Assuming the margins of error were calculated the same way, which of the following best explains why the first sample obtained a smaller margin of error than the second sample?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The first sample contained more ovens than the second sample.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The first sample contained fewer ovens than the second sample.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The first sample took more time on average to preheat to 325°F than the second sample.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The first sample took less time on average to preheat to 325°F than the second sample.

whyCorrect: With the margins of error calculated the same way, the one that comes out smaller belongs to the larger sample — more data means a more precise estimate. The first sample's margin is 1 minute against the second's 2.2 minutes, so the first sample must have had more ovens in it.

whyWrong.B: This inverts the rule. Fewer ovens would have produced the larger margin of error.
whyWrong.C: The size of the estimated average does not set the margin of error, and it is false here anyway — the first sample's average, 15.2, is the smaller of the two.
whyWrong.D: It is true that 15.2 is less than 15.4, but that difference is not what makes a margin of error small. Only the sample size explains it.

note: Same template as ma2 Research organizing #3 (town manager, 8.3% vs 6.7%); do not place both in one test.

stem: A survey was conducted in Madison to estimate the percent of adult residents who support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town. Based on the survey, it is estimated that 40% of all adult residents of Madison support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town, with an associated margin of error of 6%. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all adult residents of Madison?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Madison who support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town are between 34% and 46%.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The addition of streetlights at every corner in the town is supported by exactly 34% of all adult residents of Madison.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Madison who support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town are either less than 34% or more than 46%.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The addition of streetlights at every corner in the town is supported by more than 46% of all adult residents of Madison.

whyCorrect: Step the margin of error off either side of the estimate: 40 − 6 = 34 and 40 + 6 = 46. Those two percentages bound the plausible values for the true level of support.

whyWrong.B: 34% is simply the lower endpoint. An interval estimate never asserts an exact population value.
whyWrong.C: These are the values outside the interval, which the survey makes less plausible, not more.
whyWrong.D: 46% is the upper endpoint, so figures above it lie outside what the survey supports.

note: Same template as ma2 Research organizing #10 (Franklin, 77% ± 5%); do not place both in one test.

stem: A group of 40 employees selected at random from all the employees at a company were surveyed about the number of books they read last year. From the data collected, it was estimated that the mean number of books employees at the company read last year is 6.8, with an associated margin of error of 1.1. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.content: It is plausible that the actual mean number of books employees at the company read last year is less than 5.7.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It is plausible that the actual mean number of books employees at the company read last year is between 5.7 and 7.9.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It is plausible that every employee at the company read between 6.8 and 10.1 books last year.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It is plausible that the actual mean number of books employees at the company read last year is greater than 7.9.

whyCorrect: The interval runs from 6.8 − 1.1 = 5.7 to 6.8 + 1.1 = 7.9, and it is a statement about the mean for all employees. Watch that last part: the margin of error bounds the average, not the individual readers.

whyWrong.A: 5.7 is the bottom of the plausible interval, so means below it are the ones the estimate makes unlikely.
whyWrong.C: Two errors at once: the interval describes the company-wide mean, not what each employee did, and 6.8 to 10.1 is not the interval the numbers give.
whyWrong.D: 7.9 is the top of the interval, so means above it fall outside the plausible range.

stem: In the figure, \(RT = TU\), the measure of angle \(VST\) is 23° and the measure of angle \(RVS\) is 44°. What is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Work in triangle \(USV\) first. Because \(T\) lies on segment \(US\), angle \(VST\) and angle \(VSU\) are the same angle, so the angle at \(S\) is 23°. Because \(U\), \(V\), \(R\) are collinear, angle \(UVS\) = 180° − 44° = 136°. That leaves angle \(SUV\) = 180 − 136 − 23 = 21°. Now use \(RT = TU\): triangle \(RTU\) is isosceles, so its base angles at \(U\) and \(R\) are both 21°, and \(x = 180 - 21 - 21 = 138\).
note: Needs the figure. Reading of the page image: U, V, R lie on one horizontal line in that order; S is above and right of R; segment US passes through T; segment TR runs from T down to R and crosses segment VS; x° marks the angle at T between ray TU and ray TR, inside triangle RTU. Labelled "Figure not drawn to scale" is not printed for this item.

stem: A polygon has exactly 73 sides. If the measure of each of the 73 interior angles of this polygon is \((180p)^\circ\), what is the value of \(p\)?
whyCorrect: The interior angles of an \(n\)-sided polygon add to \((n-2)180^\circ\), so here they total \(71 \times 180\) degrees. All 73 angles are equal, so each one is \(\frac{71 \times 180}{73}\) degrees. Setting that equal to \(180p\) makes the 180 cancel: \(p = \frac{71}{73}\). Notice you never need to work out the angle in degrees.
note: Answer is the fraction 71/73 (about 0.9726); it is not an integer.

stem: Quadrilaterals \(PQRS\) and \(WXYZ\) are similar, where \(P\), \(Q\), and \(R\) correspond to \(W\), \(X\), and \(Y\), respectively. The measure of \(\angle S\) is 105°, \(PS = 25\), and \(WZ = 5\). What is the measure of \(\angle Z\)?

choices.label: A
choices.content: 5°

choices.label: B
choices.content: 21°

choices.label: C
choices.content: 75°

whyCorrect: Similar figures have equal corresponding angles; only the side lengths scale. Three correspondences are given, so the fourth vertices must match too: \(S\) corresponds to \(Z\). Therefore \(\angle Z = \angle S = 105^\circ\). The lengths 25 and 5 are there to tempt you into scaling the angle, which similarity never does.

whyWrong.A: 5 is the length \(WZ\), not an angle measure.
whyWrong.B: 21° is 105 ÷ 5, applying the side ratio to the angle. Angles are unchanged by a dilation, so they are never divided by the scale factor.
whyWrong.C: 75° is the supplement of 105°. Corresponding angles in similar figures are equal, not supplementary.

stem: Two lines intersect at exactly one point, forming two acute angles and two obtuse angles. The measure of one of these angles is \((9x - 190)^\circ\). Which of the following could NOT be the sum of the measures of any two of these angles?
whyCorrect: Call the given angle \(a = 9x - 190\). Two intersecting lines make only two distinct measures: \(a\) twice (vertical angles) and \(180 - a\) twice. So there are exactly three possible sums of two angles: \(2a = 18x - 380\), \(a + (180 - a) = 180\), and \(2(180 - a) = 360 - (18x - 380) = -18x + 740\). Choice A, \(-18x + 380\), matches none of these. The trap is that it looks like \(2a\) with the sign flipped, but flipping the sign of \(2a\) is not one of the sums.

whyWrong.B: This is the sum of the two angles that each measure \(180 - a\): \(360 - (18x - 380) = -18x + 740\).
whyWrong.C: This is \(2a\), the sum of the pair of vertical angles equal to the given one.
whyWrong.D: This is an angle plus its neighbour on a straight line, which always totals 180°.

whyCorrect: Similarity scales lengths but leaves angles alone. Three of the four correspondences are stated, so the remaining vertices pair up as well: \(S\) with \(Z\). Hence \(\angle Z = \angle S = 135^\circ\), and the side lengths 45 and 9 are irrelevant to the angle.

whyWrong.B: 27° is 135 ÷ 5, dividing the angle by the scale factor. Dilating a figure never changes an angle.

whyCorrect: The interior angles of an \(n\)-gon sum to \((n-2)180^\circ\), so all 83 angles together make \(81 \times 180\) degrees. Each equal angle is \(\frac{81 \times 180}{83}\), and setting that equal to \(180p\) cancels the 180, leaving \(p = \frac{81}{83}\).

stem: Quadrilateral \(P'Q'R'S'\) is similar to quadrilateral \(PQRS\), where \(P\), \(Q\), \(R\), and \(S\) correspond to \(P'\), \(Q'\), \(R'\), and \(S'\), respectively. The measure of angle \(P\) is 45°, the measure of angle \(Q\) is 70°, and the measure of angle \(R\) is 90°. The length of each side of \(P'Q'R'S'\) is 3 times the length of each corresponding side of \(PQRS\). What is the measure of angle \(P'\)?

choices.label: A
choices.content: 15°

choices.label: B
choices.content: 45°

choices.label: C
choices.content: 60°

whyCorrect: Enlarging a figure by a scale factor stretches every length but leaves every angle exactly as it was. \(P'\) corresponds to \(P\), so the measure of angle \(P'\) is the same 45°. The measures of angles \(Q\) and \(R\) and the scale factor 3 are all there to distract.

whyWrong.A: 15° is 45 ÷ 3, applying the scale factor to the angle. Similarity never scales angles.
whyWrong.C: 60° does not come from any correct step; it would need the angles to change, which similarity forbids.
whyWrong.D: 135° is 45 × 3, multiplying the angle by the scale factor — the same mistake as A in the opposite direction.

stem: In triangle \(PQR\), \(\overline{QR}\) is extended to point \(S\). The measure of \(\angle PQR\) is 142°, and the measure of \(\angle PRS\) is 166°. What is the measure of \(\angle QPR\)?

choices.label: A
choices.content: 14°

choices.label: B
choices.content: 19°

choices.label: C
choices.content: 24°

choices.label: D
choices.content: 38°

whyCorrect: Because \(\overline{QR}\) is extended to \(S\), the points \(Q\), \(R\), \(S\) lie on one line, so \(\angle PRQ\) and \(\angle PRS\) are supplementary: \(\angle PRQ = 180 - 166 = 14^\circ\). Now the three angles of triangle \(PQR\) add to 180°, so \(\angle QPR = 180 - 142 - 14 = 24^\circ\).

whyWrong.A: 14° is \(\angle PRQ\), the angle you find on the way, not the angle at \(P\).
whyWrong.B: 19° does not come from any correct step here.
whyWrong.D: 38° is 180 − 142, treating \(\angle PQR\) as if it had a supplement inside the triangle. Only the angle at \(R\) has a supplement in this figure, because only \(\overline{QR}\) is extended.

stem: In triangle \(PQR\), the measure of angle \(P\) is \((3x + 5)^\circ\), the measure of angle \(Q\) is \((2x + 9)^\circ\), and the measure of angle \(R\) is \((4y + 5)^\circ\). If side \(QR\) is extended through point \(R\) to point \(S\), and the measure of angle \(PRS\) is \((x + y)^\circ\), what is the value of \(x + y\)?
whyCorrect: You need two equations. First, the three angles of the triangle add to 180: \((3x+5) + (2x+9) + (4y+5) = 180\), which simplifies to \(5x + 4y = 161\). Second, \(\angle PRS\) is the supplement of angle \(R\) because \(Q\), \(R\), \(S\) are collinear: \(x + y = 180 - (4y + 5)\), i.e. \(x + 5y = 175\). Solving gives \(x = 5\) and \(y = 34\), so \(x + y = 39\). (Check: the angles are 20°, 19° and 141°, and 20 + 19 = 39 is the exterior angle at \(R\), exactly as the exterior angle theorem predicts.)

stem: In \(\triangle JKL\), the measures of both \(\angle J\) and \(\angle K\) are equal, and the measure of \(\angle L\) is 134°. What is the measure of \(\angle J\)?

choices.label: B
choices.content: 46°

choices.label: C
choices.content: 67°

choices.label: D

whyCorrect: The three angles total 180°, so \(\angle J\) and \(\angle K\) together make 180 − 134 = 46°. They are equal, so each is 46 ÷ 2 = 23°.

whyWrong.B: 46° is the combined measure of both remaining angles. You still have to halve it.

stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of these eight angles is \((7x - 250)^\circ\). The sum of the measures of four of the eight angles is \(k\). Which of the following could NOT be equivalent to \(k\), for all values of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: With a transversal across two parallel lines there are only two distinct angle measures: \(a = 7x - 250\) appears four times and \(180 - a\) appears four times. So any four of the eight angles consist of \(m\) copies of \(a\) and \(4 - m\) copies of \(180 - a\), giving exactly five possible totals: \(4a = 28x - 1{,}000\); \(3a + (180-a) = 14x - 320\); \(2a + 2(180-a) = 360\); \(a + 3(180-a) = -14x + 1{,}040\); and \(4(180-a) = -28x + 1{,}720\). Choice A, \(-14x + 1{,}540\), is not on that list — it has the right \(x\)-coefficient but the wrong constant.

whyWrong.B: This is three copies of \(a\) plus one of \(180 - a\).
whyWrong.C: This is all four of the angles equal to \(180 - a\).
whyWrong.D: This is two of each, and it is the reason the value can be free of \(x\) at all: \(a + (180 - a) = 180\) twice.

stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is \((7x - 619)^\circ\). The sum of the measure of one of the acute and three of the obtuse angles is \((-14x + w)^\circ\). What is the value of \(w\)?
whyCorrect: Every obtuse angle here is the supplement of every acute one, so if the acute angle is \(a = 7x - 619\), each obtuse angle is \(180 - a\). One acute plus three obtuse is \(a + 3(180 - a) = 540 - 2a\). Substituting: \(540 - 2(7x - 619) = 540 - 14x + 1{,}238 = -14x + 1{,}778\). Matching this against \(-14x + w\) gives \(w = 1{,}778\).

stem: In the figure shown, point \(T\) lies on segment \(SW\), and segment \(TU\) is parallel to segment \(VW\). The measure of angle \(V\) is 26°, and the measure of angle \(STU\) is 74°. What is the value of \(p - r\)?
whyCorrect: Line \(SW\) cuts the two parallel segments \(TU\) and \(VW\), so angle \(STU\) and angle \(SWV\) are corresponding angles: \(r = 74\). Segment \(UV\) cuts the same pair of parallels, so angle \(TUV\) and angle \(UVW\) are same-side interior angles and add to 180°: \(p = 180 - 26 = 154\). Therefore \(p - r = 154 - 74 = 80\). (Check with the quadrilateral \(TUVW\): its angles are 106, 154, 26 and 74, totalling 360.)
note: Needs the figure. Reading of the page image: \(TUVW\) is a trapezoid with \(W\) bottom-left, \(V\) bottom-right, \(T\) upper-left and \(U\) upper-right; \(TU\) is parallel to \(WV\); \(S\) sits above \(T\) on the extension of \(WT\). \(p^\circ\) labels the interior angle at \(U\) (angle \(TUV\)) and \(r^\circ\) labels the interior angle at \(W\) (angle \(TWV\)). Derived values: \(p = 154\), \(r = 74\).

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

whyCorrect: Track the correspondence: \(A\) matches \(D\) and \(B\) matches \(E\), so the remaining vertices match too — \(C\) with \(F\). Angle \(C\) is what is left in triangle \(ABC\) after the right angle and the 62° angle: \(180 - 90 - 62 = 28^\circ\). Congruence makes angle \(F\) equal to that, 28°.

stem: In triangle \(RST\), the measure of angle \(R\) is 10 degrees and the measure of angle \(T\) is 50 degrees. Point \(L\) lies on \(\overline{RS}\), point \(K\) lies on \(\overline{ST}\), and \(\overline{LK}\) is parallel to \(\overline{RT}\). What is the measure, in degrees, of angle \(SKL\)? (Disregard the degree symbol when entering your answer.)
whyCorrect: Side \(ST\) is a transversal cutting the parallel segments \(\overline{LK}\) and \(\overline{RT}\). Angle \(SKL\) at \(K\) and angle \(STR\) at \(T\) are corresponding angles, so they are equal, making angle \(SKL\) = 50°. Another way to see it: \(\triangle SLK\) and \(\triangle SRT\) share the angle at \(S\) and have parallel third sides, so they are similar and their angles match up. The measure of angle \(R\) is not needed.

stem: In the figure shown, point \(D\) lies on \(\overline{AB}\), point \(E\) lies on \(\overline{CB}\), and line segments \(AC\) and \(DE\) are parallel. The measure of angle \(ACB\) is 58°, and \(AB = 1.5DB\). What is the measure, in degrees, of angle \(DEB\)? (Disregard the degree symbol when entering your answer.)
whyCorrect: \(\overline{CB}\) crosses the two parallel segments \(\overline{DE}\) and \(\overline{AC}\), so angle \(DEB\) and angle \(ACB\) are corresponding angles and therefore equal: 58°. The ratio \(AB = 1.5DB\) fixes how much smaller the inner triangle is, but a scale factor never changes an angle, so it plays no part in the answer.
note: The book shows this only as a figure; the sentence placing D on AB and E on CB has been written into the stem so the question stands without the picture.

stem: In the figure shown, \(B\) and \(C\) lie on \(\overline{AD}\), \(E\) lies on \(\overline{DF}\), and \(\overline{CE}\) is parallel to \(\overline{AF}\). Which of the following is enough to prove that \(\triangle BDE\) is similar to \(\triangle EDC\)?
whyCorrect: The two triangles already share the angle at \(D\), so one more matching pair settles it. In the correspondence \(B \to E\), \(D \to D\), \(E \to C\), that pair is angle \(DEB\) with angle \(DCE\). Angle \(DEB\) is split by \(\overline{EC}\) into \(x\) and \(s\), so it measures \(s + x\), and angle \(DCE\) is \(w\). Because \(\overline{CE} \parallel \overline{AF}\), corresponding angles give \(w = y\). So the needed condition, \(s + x = w\), is the same as \(s + x = y\).

whyWrong.A: The parallel lines already force \(w = y\) and \(x = z\), so this reduces to \(w = x\) — it makes \(\triangle DCE\) isosceles but says nothing about where \(B\) sits.
whyWrong.B: This reduces to \(w + x = w + x\), which is true no matter what. A statement that is always true cannot prove anything.
whyWrong.C: Since \(x = z\), this reduces to \(s = 0\), which would mean \(\overline{EB}\) and \(\overline{EC}\) are the same ray — impossible in this figure.

note: Needs the figure. Reading of the page image: \(\triangle ADF\) has \(D\) at the top, \(A\) bottom-left, \(F\) bottom-right; \(B\) and \(C\) lie on \(\overline{AD}\) with \(C\) above \(B\); \(E\) lies on \(\overline{DF}\); \(\overline{CE}\) is drawn parallel to \(\overline{AF}\) and \(\overline{BE}\) is also drawn. Labels: \(w^\circ\) is angle \(DCE\), \(x^\circ\) is angle \(DEC\), \(s^\circ\) is angle \(CEB\), \(y^\circ\) is angle \(DAF\) at \(A\), \(z^\circ\) is angle \(AFD\) at \(F\).

stem: A triangle has a base length of 82 centimeters and a height of 164 centimeters. What is the area, in square centimeters, of the triangle?
whyCorrect: Area of a triangle is \(\frac{1}{2}bh\). Here that is \(\frac{1}{2}(82)(164) = 41 \times 164 = 6{,}724\) square centimeters.

whyWrong.A: 246 is 82 + 164, adding the two lengths instead of multiplying them.
whyWrong.B: 3,362 is \(\frac{1}{2}\) of 82 times \(\frac{1}{2}\) of 164 — the one-half applied twice.
whyWrong.D: 13,448 is \(82 \times 164\), the area of a rectangle with those dimensions. A triangle is half of it.
